title: Diplomatic and Formal Language
description: Master the specialised register of diplomatic communication, international protocol, formal oratory, and high-level institutional discourse. This course covers the language of treaties, diplomatic correspondence, international negotiations, ceremonial speeches, and formal procedural communication at C2 level.

lessons.title: Diplomatic Communication: Precision, Ambiguity, and Euphemism

content.content: {"time":1700000131000,"blocks":[{"id":"aB1cD2eF3g","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Diplomatic language operates within a paradox: it demands both extreme precision (to create binding international commitments) and strategic ambiguity (to enable parties with genuinely incompatible positions to reach agreements). This tension defines diplomatic discourse at every level, from bilateral negotiations to UN Security Council resolutions."}},{"id":"hI4jK5lM6n","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Constructive ambiguity — deliberately vague or ambiguous language inserted into agreements to allow each party to interpret the outcome as consistent with its position — is a recognised diplomatic technique. The language of UN Resolution 242 ('withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' — omitting the definite article 'the' before 'territories') is a famous example."}},{"id":"oP7qR8sT9u","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Diplomatic language is characterised by: formal register (avoiding contractions, colloquialisms, and emotive vocabulary); indirect expression (preference for passive constructions, nominalisations, and impersonal structures); hedging (extensive use of modal verbs and qualifying phrases); and formulaic courtesy (fixed expressions that signal respect while maintaining professional distance)."}},{"id":"vW0xY1zA2b","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Diplomatic euphemisms: Direct accusations are rarely made in formal diplomacy. Instead: 'We have concerns about…' (= we strongly object to); 'We urge restraint' (= stop doing what you are doing); 'frank and candid discussions' (= heated disagreement); 'exploratory talks' (= preliminary discussions with no commitment); 'a full and frank exchange of views' (= a serious disagreement without resolution)."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: Both parties engaged in frank and candid discussions and agreed to continue exploratory talks at the earliest opportunity.

pairs.right: Deliberately vague language allowing different parties to claim success
Diplomatic expression meaning: we strongly object to this
Diplomatic expression meaning: stop doing what you are doing

questions.text: What is 'constructive ambiguity' in diplomatic language?
options: A technique for writing legally binding treaties with precise terms
Deliberately vague language that allows different parties to interpret an agreement as consistent with their own positions
The use of formal euphemisms to avoid causing offence
The practice of providing multiple translations of a key document

topics.title: Module 2: Treaty Language and International Law

lessons.title: The Language of International Agreements and Resolutions

content.content: {"time":1700000132000,"blocks":[{"id":"cD3eF4gH5i","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"International treaties and resolutions have a highly formalised linguistic structure. UN Security Council resolutions, for example, follow a strict template: preambular paragraphs (beginning with present participles: Recalling, Noting, Affirming, Welcoming, Alarmed by, Deeply concerned…) followed by operative paragraphs (beginning with verbs in the present tense: Decides, Demands, Urges, Calls upon, Encourages, Authorises…)."}},{"id":"jK6lM7nO8p","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The operative verb chosen in a Security Council resolution is legally significant. 'Decides' creates binding obligations under Chapter VII of the UN Charter; 'demands' is strong but not necessarily binding; 'urges' and 'calls upon' are hortatory rather than binding; 'encourages' and 'welcomes' are purely exhortatory. Drafting states negotiate these distinctions with great care."}},{"id":"qR9sT0uV1w","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Treaty language features: The operative unit is the article, numbered and containing a single substantive provision. All substantive parties are defined in the opening articles. Obligations are expressed using 'shall'; permissions with 'may'; prohibitions with 'shall not'. Dispute resolution mechanisms specify the procedure (arbitration, ICJ jurisdiction, etc.)."}},{"id":"xY2zA3bC4d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Key treaty vocabulary: ratification (formal domestic approval), accession (joining an existing treaty), reservation (a state's declaration limiting its acceptance of a provision), entry into force (when a treaty becomes legally operative), denunciation (formal withdrawal), derogation (temporary suspension of obligations), jus cogens (peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted)."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: The Security Council decides that all member states shall immediately cease supplying arms to the parties in the conflict.

items.text: The Security Council ENCOURAGES member states to…
The Security Council CALLS UPON parties to refrain from…
The Security Council DEMANDS the immediate cessation of…
The Security Council WELCOMES the efforts of…
The Security Council AUTHORISES member states to use all necessary means…

guessItems.hint: Formal declaration by a state limiting its acceptance of a specific treaty provision
Peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted

questions.text: In a UN Security Council resolution, which operative verb creates legally binding obligations under the UN Charter?
options: Encourages
Calls upon
Urges
Decides

lessons.title: The Architecture of Formal Speeches: Rhetoric and Ceremony

content.content: {"time":1700000133000,"blocks":[{"id":"eF5gH6iJ7k","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Formal oratory — at state occasions, international assemblies, and institutional ceremonies — draws on the oldest traditions of rhetoric while adapting to contemporary standards of formality and decorum. The ability to write and deliver such speeches is a high-level professional skill."}},{"id":"lM8nO9pQ0r","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Classical rhetorical devices that remain central to formal oratory:"}},{"id":"sT1uV2wX3y","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Anaphora — repetition at the beginning of successive clauses: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds…' (Churchill)","Epistrophe — repetition at the end of successive clauses: 'of the people, by the people, for the people' (Lincoln)","Chiasmus — reversal of grammatical structure: 'Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country' (Kennedy)","Tricolon — a series of three parallel elements: 'Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness'","Antithesis — contrasting ideas in parallel structure: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' (Dickens)"]}},{"id":"zA4bC5dE6f","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Ceremonial speech conventions: Formal speeches at state occasions typically include: acknowledgement of dignitaries (in strict order of protocol), a statement of the occasion's significance, reference to shared values or history, a central substantive argument or narrative, and a forward-looking conclusion expressing commitment or hope."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.

pairs.right: Repetition at the beginning of successive clauses
Repetition at the end of successive clauses
Reversal of grammatical structure across two clauses
A series of three parallel elements
Contrasting ideas expressed in parallel structure

mistakeItems.text: 'We shall fight, we shall struggle, and we shall resist' — Identify the rhetorical device. [Wrong answer: antithesis]
mistakeItems.correctText: Anaphora — repetition at the beginning of successive clauses ('we shall')

mistakeItems.text: 'The more you learn, the more you realise how little you know' — Identify the device. [Wrong answer: anaphora]
mistakeItems.correctText: Antithesis — contrasting ideas expressed in a parallel structure

questions.text: Which rhetorical device does Kennedy use in 'Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country'?
options: Anaphora
Tricolon
Chiasmus
Epistrophe

topics.title: Module 4: Protocol, Ceremonial Language, and Titles

lessons.title: Diplomatic Protocol: Forms of Address and Ceremonial Conventions

content.content: {"time":1700000134000,"blocks":[{"id":"gH7iJ8kL9m","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Protocol in diplomacy refers to the system of rules, conventions, and ceremonial procedures governing the conduct of diplomatic relations. Correct forms of address, precedence, and ceremonial language are not mere formalities — they signal respect for the institutions and individuals represented."}},{"id":"nO0pQ1rS2t","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Forms of address (selected):"}},{"id":"uV3wX4yZ5a","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Heads of state / presidents: Your Excellency, Mr./Madam President","Prime ministers and senior ministers: Your Excellency, Prime Minister","Ambassadors: Your Excellency, Ambassador","In formal correspondence: I have the honour to inform Your Excellency… / I avail myself of this opportunity to renew to Your Excellency the assurances of my highest consideration. (standard formal valediction)","Monarchs: Your Majesty (on first reference), Sir/Ma'am thereafter","Judges of international courts: The Honourable, President/Judge [Name]"]}},{"id":"bC6dE7fG8h","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Note verbale is the most common form of written diplomatic communication: an impersonal third-person note ('The Embassy of [Country] presents its compliments to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and has the honour to inform…'). The impersonal structure and absence of salutation and signature are defining features of this genre."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: The Embassy of the Republic presents its compliments to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and has the honour to inform it of the following.

pairs.english: I avail myself of this opportunity to renew to Your Excellency the assurances of my highest consideration.
pairs.russian: Пользуясь настоящим случаем, прошу Вас, г-н Посол, принять заверения в моём самом высоком уважении.

pairs.english: The Embassy of [Country] presents its compliments to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and has the honour to transmit the following note verbale.
pairs.russian: Посольство [Страны] свидетельствует своё уважение Министерству иностранных дел и имеет честь передать нижеследующую вербальную ноту.

questions.text: What is a 'note verbale' in diplomatic communication?
options: An oral communication delivered at a press conference
A formal impersonal written diplomatic communication in the third person
A personal letter from one foreign minister to another
A verbal agreement that has not yet been put in writing

lessons.title: Strategic Language in High-Stakes Diplomatic Negotiations

content.content: {"time":1700000135000,"blocks":[{"id":"iJ9kL0mN1o","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Diplomatic negotiations at the highest level deploy a sophisticated interplay of signalling, ambiguity, face-saving devices, and strategic framing. Understanding the pragmatics of high-level negotiation English — what is meant beyond what is said — is a C2-level skill."}},{"id":"pQ2rS3tU4v","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Face-saving language is essential when parties need to accept compromise without appearing to capitulate. Formulas include: 'In the spirit of constructive dialogue…' / 'Without prejudice to our fundamental position…' / 'We are prepared to consider a creative solution that addresses the core concerns of both parties.'"}},{"id":"wX5yZ6aB7c","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Signalling intent without commitment: Diplomats often need to indicate willingness to move without formally committing to a position: 'Exploratory conversations have been constructive.' / 'We remain open to further discussion on modalities.' / 'There may be room for a mutually acceptable arrangement if the concerns of both sides are properly addressed.'"}},{"id":"dE8fG9hI0j","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Managing disagreement without rupture: 'We take note of your position, while maintaining our own.' / 'We respectfully disagree, and we believe this matter merits further reflection.' / 'We are unable to accept the current formulation, but we remain committed to finding a solution.'"}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: We are prepared to consider a creative solution that adequately addresses the core concerns of both delegations.

content.instructions: Read the following diplomatic phrase aloud with appropriate formal, measured delivery
content.targetPhrase: Without prejudice to our fundamental position, we are prepared to explore possible accommodations that address the concerns of both delegations.

pairs.english: We take note of your delegation's position, while maintaining our own long-standing view on this matter.
pairs.russian: Мы принимаем к сведению позицию вашей делегации, сохраняя при этом нашу давнюю точку зрения по данному вопросу.

pairs.english: There may be room for a mutually acceptable arrangement, provided the core interests of both parties are adequately addressed.
pairs.russian: Возможно, существует пространство для взаимоприемлемого урегулирования при условии надлежащего учёта основных интересов обеих сторон.

questions.text: What is the function of 'face-saving language' in diplomatic negotiations?
options: To insult the opposing delegation indirectly
To allow a party to accept compromise without appearing to capitulate or lose prestige
To terminate negotiations without reaching an agreement
To disguise the true legal meaning of a treaty provision
